# Forensic Dossier — Capgemini SE (CAP.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from eight consecutive quarterly calls (full-year 2024 reported February 2025 through full-year 2025 reported February 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Capgemini is Europe's largest information-technology services and consulting firm — it sells the labor and software to help big companies move to the cloud, modernize core systems, and now deploy artificial intelligence (AI). Across these eight quarters the story travels a clear arc: **from "managing a downturn" to "buying our way into the next growth wave."**

At the start (full-year 2024, reported February 2025) the tone is defensive. Chief executive Aiman Ezzat opens by conceding "the market proved weaker than we anticipated," with revenue down 2% at constant currency, manufacturing and France the soft spots, and clients refusing to "increase their discretionary spend." The emphasis is on resilience — holding the operating margin at 13.3% despite a falling top line — and on a self-help program ("targeted actions") launched in the third quarter of 2024 to "unlock potential at every level."

Through 2025 the narrative shifts from defense to a gradual, quarter-by-quarter recovery. Each call repeats the same refrain — "performance continues to improve through the first half," growth "improved steadily" — culminating in a genuinely strong fourth quarter (constant-currency growth of 10.6%). But the honest reader sees that **most of that acceleration is bought, not earned**: management discloses about 6.5 points of the Q4 growth came from "scope" (acquisitions), "driven primarily by WNS and Cloud4C." Organic growth, the part that reflects the underlying business, finished 2025 barely positive.

The thesis expands twice along the way. First, a new growth pillar — **"Intelligent Operations,"** the AI-powered remaking of business-process outsourcing — is introduced and then made concrete with the July 2025 acquisition of WNS (a large Indian business-process company). Second, two genuinely new demand themes appear and grow louder each quarter: **European defense** ("about €1 billion of revenue ... up 12%") and **digital sovereignty** (clients wanting their data kept on home soil). Generative AI moves from ~4% of bookings (full-year 2024) to over 8% (Q3 2025) — a real, rising contributor.

Quietly dropped or de-emphasized: the early-2025 hand-wringing over tariffs and "Liberation Day" client caution simply fades as the year proves benign. And the "1-to-2 points of M&A" framing narrows to "around 1 point" of bolt-ons — right before the company does the opposite and swallows WNS, a transformational deal that adds ~6.5 points of scope.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | Where it appears | What the financials show | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Strong resilience of the operating model"; margin held at 13.3% | Every call | Net margin 7.1%, gross margin 25.1% (stable); operating margin genuinely steady ~13.3% | **Matches.** Margin discipline is real and is the company's strongest credibility anchor. |
| Growth "improving steadily" through 2025 | H1, Q3, FY 2025 | Reported revenue: €22.10B (2024) → €22.46B (2025), +1.7% reported. 3-year revenue compound growth just +0.7% | **Poorer than narrated.** The "improvement" is real in trend but the absolute base is flat-to-stagnant; organic growth finished barely positive. |
| Q4 constant-currency growth of 10.6% | FY 2025 | Management itself discloses ~6.5 points is acquired "scope" | **Honest, but the headline flatters.** Organic Q4 was ~4%; the double-digit print is mostly bought. |
| Free cash flow "strong" and on target (~€1.95B) | All calls | Annual organic free cash flow ~€1.95B delivered; screener trailing-twelve-month free cash flow €4.31B (gross), price-to-free-cash-flow ~6.7x | **Matches.** Cash conversion is a genuine strength and the core of the value case. |
| WNS synergies "on track" — €100-140M revenue, €50-70M cost by end-2027; first €600M mega-deal already won | FY 2025 | Headcount jumped 23% year-on-year to ~421,000 (mostly WNS); net debt €6.43B (total debt €9.46B less €3.03B cash) | **Unproven but plausible.** The deal is closed and integration is early; the €600M deal is a real, datable proof point, but synergies are a 2027 promise, not delivered. |
| Earnings per share growing | Trajectory | Normalized EPS €12.23 (2024) → €12.95 (2025), +5.8%; screener basic EPS €9.13, down 3.6% year-on-year | **Mixed.** "Normalized" EPS grows; reported/basic EPS dipped, dragged by restructuring and acquisition costs. The gap between the two numbers is the tell. |
| "Fit for Growth" will fund the future | FY 2025 | ~€700M restructuring envelope over two years, majority in 2026; ~€200M extra cash outflow in 2026 | **A cost, not yet a benefit.** This is the near-term drag on free cash flow. |

The cross-check verdict: **the financials corroborate the margin and cash-flow story, but expose the growth story as substantially acquired rather than organic.** Return on invested capital (ROIC) of 9.0% sits roughly at or only modestly above the firm's cost of capital — adequate, not excellent, and the WNS deal (a lower-revenue-per-head business funded partly with debt) is unlikely to lift it in the near term.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Rising (off a low base).**

- *Full-year 2024 (Feb 2025) — defensive:* "the market proved weaker than we anticipated," "clients did not increase their discretionary spend." Cautious, explaining a miss.
- *Q1 2025 — cautiously better:* "slightly better than our initial expectation," but heavily hedged on tariffs — "we remain extremely cautious of any potential development."
- *H1 2025 — turning:* "Our performance continues to improve," "returned to positive constant currency growth in Q2." Management raises the low end of guidance but explicitly "retain[s] the cautious stance."
- *Q3 2025 — confident:* "Q3 was a strong quarter for the group better than expected ... improvement has been pretty broad-based." The most offensive (growth-oriented) language of the series.
- *FY 2025 (Feb 2026) — assertive:* "Capgemini delivered a solid set of results," revenue "above the upgraded guidance," plus a confident, almost combative defense against AI-disruption fears (the pointed Palantir rebuttal — "don't stay on the headline").

The shift from defensive ("efficiency, cost, macro") to offensive ("AI, Intelligent Operations, sovereignty, defense") language is real and consistent. Guidance became *more* specific over time, not less — a credibility positive.

## 4. GUIDANCE CREDIBILITY

**Reliability: High.**

Management set a 2025 framework early (constant-currency revenue −2% to +2%, margin 13.3-13.5%, free cash flow ~€1.9B) and then *narrowed it upward* through the year (to −1% to +1%, then "above the upgraded guidance" at year-end) while hitting margin and cash flow on the nose. The screener's earnings-beat record (beat 6 of 7 quarters, 86%) corroborates a modest, deliverable-guidance culture. There is a mild **sandbagging pattern** — the repeated "between realistic and conservative" framing and the habit of guiding cautiously then beating — which is a positive sign for a value setup. The one honest blemish: they guided "around 1 point" of acquisitions and then did a transformational deal, so the *organic* picture has to be read carefully against the headline.

## 5. ANALYST PRESSURE POINTS

Recurring questions management circled rather than answered crisply:
- **How much AI actually deflates pricing.** Analysts (BNP, Jefferies) pressed repeatedly on whether generative AI lowers the cost of delivery and forces price give-backs. Ezzat's answers are real but evasive on magnitude — "some of that is being passed to customers ... it's not yet, again, large scale." This is the central bear question and management never quantifies it.
- **Organic vs. acquired growth.** Analysts kept separating the M&A contribution from underlying demand; management consistently steered back to the headline.
- **France and manufacturing/auto.** Pressed every quarter. Management called the France "trough" passed in Q1 2025, yet France was "still challenging at year-end." Auto is candidly conceded as a structural, not cyclical, drag — "we don't expect to see a rebound in auto."
- **The buyback's true share-count impact.** Jefferies pushed twice on how much of the €2B buyback offsets dilution versus shrinks the count; management would not commit ("it depends on the timing").

## 6. RED FLAGS / GREEN FLAGS

🔴 **Red flags**
- *Growth is bought, not earned.* ~6.5 points of Q4 2025 growth is acquired scope; organic growth is barely positive on a flat three-year revenue base.
- *Reported EPS fell* (−3.6% year-on-year on the screener's basis) even as "normalized" EPS rose — the adjustments are doing work.
- *Net debt of €6.43B* now sits on the balance sheet after WNS, in a higher-for-longer rate world; this is a liability that must be subtracted in any valuation, not a cushion.
- *The core secular question is unanswered:* AI may automate the very labor-arbitrage hours this business bills for. Management's confidence here is asserted, not demonstrated.

🟢 **Green flags**
- *Margin and cash flow are genuinely durable* — held flat through a two-year demand downturn.
- *Tone and underlying momentum are improving* quarter after quarter, broad-based across geographies and sectors by Q3 2025.
- *Two real new demand vectors* (European defense double-digit growth; sovereignty) that are structural tailwinds, not hype.
- *Honest, deliverable guidance* with a sandbagging bias and an 86% beat rate.
- *Shareholder returns* — a €2B buyback accelerating in 2026 plus ~35% dividend payout.

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The vocabulary migrated** from "cloud/digital" (2024) to "Agentic AI / Intelligent Operations / sovereignty / defense" (2025-26) — management is repositioning the narrative ahead of the financials, which is either prescient or defensive depending on whether the AI-displacement fear proves real.
- **"Revenue per head" candor.** Ezzat openly admits WNS *lowers* revenue per employee today and bets it rises "over the midterm" via AI leverage — an unusually frank acknowledgment that the deal dilutes a key efficiency metric first.
- **The Palantir rebuttal** (FY 2025) is the most revealing moment: management felt compelled to publicly argue that AI will *not* collapse large-enterprise transformation work. You only mount that defense when the market is pricing the opposite — which is exactly what the depressed multiple says.
- **"Fit for Growth"** is corporate language for a sizeable workforce reset (~€700M) driven explicitly by "evolution ... from AI" — a tacit admission that AI changes the headcount model.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE, tilting toward STRENGTHENING.** This is a well-run, cash-generative franchise that has navigated a two-year demand trough with its margins and credibility intact and is now repositioning — via WNS and an AI-services pivot — toward the next cycle. Management is honest and delivers on what it controls (margin, cash, guidance).

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** *Is the depressed multiple a fear-print or a value trap?* The whole investment case turns on whether generative AI is a tool that Capgemini sells (bullish — it lifts demand for transformation work) or a force that automates the billable labor-hours its model depends on (bearish — terminal-value erosion). The financials don't yet settle it: returns are merely adequate (ROIC 9.0%), organic growth is flat, and the recent growth is acquired.

**Moat:** intangible/relationship and scale-based — deep client entrenchment, vendor-consolidation winner status ("if you're big, you stay in and you win"), and a top-tier partner ecosystem. But it is a **narrow** moat with thin switching costs relative to true software lock-in, and the returns evidence (ROIC ~9%, stable-not-rising margins, flat organic growth) points to a moat that is holding, not widening. **Moat trend: stable**, with a credible erosion risk if AI deflates bill-rates faster than volume grows.

**Secular threat:** the labor-arbitrage / AI-automation-of-IT-services theme is **material** — a real, debatable risk to the terminal economics of billing labor-hours at a spread — but not yet *terminal*: the firm is positioning to sell AI transformation, defense and sovereignty are genuine offsetting tailwinds, and demand for large, complex enterprise change has so far proven sticky. The cheapness is therefore best read as a **fear-print with a real (but not fatal) secular overhang**, not a melting-base value trap — provided organic growth re-accelerates and AI proves additive rather than substitutive.

# Forensic Dossier — Capgemini SE (CAP.PA)

*A deep dive on management and the setup, built from eight consecutive quarterly calls (full-year 2024 reported February 2025 through full-year 2025 reported February 2026) cross-checked against the screener's hard financials.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Capgemini is Europe's largest information-technology services and consulting firm — it sells the labor and software to help big companies move to the cloud, modernize core systems, and now deploy artificial intelligence (AI). At the start (full-year 2024, reported February 2025) the tone is defensive. Chief executive Aiman Ezzat opens by conceding "the market proved weaker than we anticipated," with revenue down 2% at constant currency, manufacturing and France the soft spots, and clients refusing to "increase their discretionary spend." The emphasis is on resilience — holding the operating margin at 13.3% despite a falling top line — and on a self-help program ("targeted actions") launched in the third quarter of 2024 to "unlock potential at every level."

Through 2025 the narrative shifts from defense to a gradual, quarter-by-quarter recovery. Each call repeats the same refrain — "performance continues to improve through the first half," growth "improved steadily" — culminating in a genuinely strong fourth quarter (constant-currency growth of 10.6%). But the honest reader sees that **most of that acceleration is bought, not earned**: management discloses about 6.5 points of the Q4 growth came from "scope" (acquisitions), "driven primarily by WNS and Cloud4C." Organic growth, the part that reflects the underlying business, finished 2025 barely positive.

The thesis expands twice along the way. First, a new growth pillar — **"Intelligent Operations,"** the AI-powered remaking of business-process outsourcing — is introduced and then made concrete with the July 2025 acquisition of WNS (a large Indian business-process company). Second, two genuinely new demand themes appear and grow louder each quarter: **European defense** ("about €1 billion of revenue ... up 12%") and **digital sovereignty** (clients wanting their data kept on home soil). Generative AI moves from ~4% of bookings (full-year 2024) to over 8% (Q3 2025) — a real, rising contributor.

Quietly dropped or de-emphasized: the early-2025 hand-wringing over tariffs and "Liberation Day" client caution simply fades as the year proves benign. **Classification: STABLE, tilting toward STRENGTHENING.** This is a well-run, cash-generative franchise that has navigated a two-year demand trough with its margins and credibility intact and is now repositioning — via WNS and an AI-services pivot — toward the next cycle. **Reliability: High.**

- **The vocabulary migrated** from "cloud/digital" (2024) to "Agentic AI / Intelligent Operations / sovereignty / defense" (2025-26) — management is repositioning the narrative ahead of the financials, which is either prescient or defensive depending on whether the AI-displacement fear proves real.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: STABLE, tilting toward STRENGTHENING.** This is a well-run, cash-generative franchise that has navigated a two-year demand trough with its margins and credibility intact and is now repositioning — via WNS and an AI-services pivot — toward the next cycle. The financials don't yet settle it: returns are merely adequate (ROIC 9.0%), organic growth is flat, and the recent growth is acquired.

**Moat:** intangible/relationship and scale-based — deep client entrenchment, vendor-consolidation winner status ("if you're big, you stay in and you win"), and a top-tier partner ecosystem. But it is a **narrow** moat with thin switching costs relative to true software lock-in, and the returns evidence (ROIC ~9%, stable-not-rising margins, flat organic growth) points to a moat that is holding, not widening. **Moat trend: stable**, with a credible erosion risk if AI deflates bill-rates faster than volume grows.

**Secular threat:** the labor-arbitrage / AI-automation-of-IT-services theme is **material** — a real, debatable risk to the terminal economics of billing labor-hours at a spread — but not yet *terminal*: the firm is positioning to sell AI transformation, defense and sovereignty are genuine offsetting tailwinds, and demand for large, complex enterprise change has so far proven sticky. The cheapness is therefore best read as a **fear-print with a real (but not fatal) secular overhang**, not a melting-base value trap — provided organic growth re-accelerates and AI proves additive rather than substitutive.

# Capgemini SE (CAP.PA) — Forensic Dossier

*Interrogator note, prepared for the investment committee. Six consecutive quarterly calls, February 2025 through February 2026, cross-checked against the screener's financial trajectory. All figures in euros unless stated. Live share price used throughout: about EUR 91.62 on Euronext Paris (13 July 2026), roughly 40% below the 12-month high near EUR 153.*

## 1. Narrative Arc

Capgemini is a French information-technology services and consulting group — it sells the labor and know-how of roughly 340,000 people to help large companies modernize their technology. Across these six calls the story travels a clean arc from apology to recovery.

The February 2025 full-year-2024 call is defensive and a little bruised: chief executive Aiman Ezzat concedes "the market proved weaker than we anticipated," with revenue down 2% at constant currency and "unexpectedly strong headwinds in the second half, notably in manufacturing and in France." The emphasis is on resilience, cost discipline, and a newly launched self-help program to "unlock potential… for fueling growth and driving efficiencies."

Each subsequent quarter tells a slightly better story. The first quarter of 2025 is "slightly better than expected" (constant-currency revenue only minus 0.4%); the second quarter returns the group to positive growth (plus 0.7%); the third quarter is "a strong quarter… better than expected" at plus 2.9%; and the February 2026 full-year call closes 2025 at plus 3.4% constant-currency growth, "above the upgraded guidance," with a very strong fourth-quarter book-to-bill (new orders divided by revenue) of 1.21.

Three growth engines are introduced or amplified along the way, and none is quietly dropped — a good sign of narrative honesty. First, generative and agentic artificial intelligence, which climbs from "close to 4%" of bookings (2024) to "over 8%" (third quarter 2025). Second, European defense and sovereignty, framed as a multi-year structural tailwind ("about EUR 1 billion of revenue in European defense, up 12%," with "further acceleration in the next 2 to 3 years"). Third, the July 2025 acquisition of WNS, a business-process-outsourcing firm, closed in the autumn and pitched as the vehicle to lead "Intelligent Operations" — running and re-engineering clients' back-office processes with AI. By February 2026 the company reports its "first mega deal of over EUR 600 million" on a "non-FTE based commercial model" (priced on outcomes, not headcount).

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The number | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Underlying performance strengthened quarter after quarter" (Feb 2026) | Constant-currency growth improved -0.4% → +0.7% → +2.9% → strong Q4; full-year +3.4% | **Matches.** The re-acceleration is real and monotonic. |
| Operating margin "resilient" and on target | 13.3% for 2025, stable year on year despite the revenue decline earlier in the cycle | **Matches**, but note it is *stable*, not expanding — the mix-shift-to-margin story has not yet lifted the headline rate. |
| Organic free cash flow "on target" | EUR 1.95 billion, in line with the ~EUR 1.9 billion guide | **Matches.** Cash conversion is dependable. |
| Normalized earnings per share growth | EUR 12.95, up 5.8% year on year | **Matches**, though most of the lift is below the revenue line (buyback, mix), not volume. |
| Returns on capital are healthy | Return on invested capital about 9%; return on equity 14.7% | **Poorer than the narrative.** A 9% return on invested capital is roughly half Accenture's ~20% and is the single weakest fundamental fact here. |
| Net debt is modest | Net debt about EUR 6.4 billion including leases (EUR 5.3 billion excluding) after funding WNS | **Richer risk than management dwells on** — leverage stepped up to buy WNS; this is a liability to subtract in any valuation, not "net cash." |

The screener's own "TTM free cash flow of EUR 4.31 billion" should be treated with caution: it is well above the company's stated organic free cash flow of EUR 1.95 billion and likely reflects reported (pre-organic-adjustment) cash flow plus WNS consolidation and working-capital timing. The durable, guide-anchored figure is closer to EUR 2 billion.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Rising, from a low base.** February 2025 is the trough of confidence — repeated hedging ("we remain cautious," "wait-and-see game"). By the third quarter of 2025 the language turns forward-leaning: "a strong quarter," "broad-based" improvement, "uniquely positioned." Management stays specific with guidance throughout — narrowing the 2025 range up as the year progressed rather than issuing vague reassurance — which reads as genuine visibility, not spin. The one persistent defensive note is France and automotive, which Ezzat never sugar-coats ("a broad weakness in France," auto "a structural change… we don't expect to see a rebound").

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**High.** The 2025 guide began at minus 2% to plus 2% constant-currency growth and was *narrowed upward* mid-year to minus 1% to plus 1%, then delivered at plus 3.4% — an under-promise-and-over-deliver pattern consistent with the screener's 86% earnings-beat rate (six of seven quarters). Margin and cash landed exactly on target. There is a mild sandbagging habit (the Q1 2026 guide of plus 8.5% to 9.5% leans on ~6.5 points of acquired scope and "traditional seasonality"). Reliability score: **High.**

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Analysts pressed hardest on three fronts, and management's answers were candid rather than evasive. (a) *Gen-AI cannibalization* — whether AI lowers Capgemini's own delivery pricing; Ezzat conceded "yes… some of that is being passed to customers" but argued it is embedded in normal annual productivity. (b) *Sales intensity* — whether the higher selling cost to drive growth is permanent; management promised it would fall "over time" without committing to a date. (c) *France and automotive* — repeatedly flagged; management's "past the trough" call in Q1 2025 proved premature, as France stayed weak (~minus 5%) into mid-year. That is the one place the narrative ran ahead of the facts.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 Return on invested capital of ~9% is low for the quality claimed and well below Accenture. 🔴 Growth is heavily scope-assisted — the strong Q4 2025 and Q1 2026 headlines carry ~6.5 points of WNS/Cloud4C acquisition, so *organic* momentum is milder than the reported rate. 🔴 A EUR 700 million "Fit for Growth" restructuring envelope signals that headcount and skills must be reshaped for AI — an admission of pressure as much as opportunity. 🔴 Gen-AI pricing give-backs are a live drag on gross margin.

🟢 Six straight quarters of improving growth, ending above raised guidance. 🟢 Dependable cash and margin delivery. 🟢 Genuine structural tailwinds in European defense (double-digit growth) and sovereignty. 🟢 The EUR 600 million outcome-priced Intelligent Operations mega-deal is early proof the WNS thesis can work. 🟢 Cheap: roughly 7 times normalized earnings and an organic free-cash-flow yield near 13%.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most important terminology shift is the move from selling *people* to selling *outcomes*. Management now stresses "non-FTE based" pricing, "revenue per head" rising over the medium term, and AI "decoupling" revenue from headcount. Read positively, Capgemini is trying to get ahead of the very force that threatens it. Read skeptically, it is telling you the old labor-arbitrage engine — billing hours at a spread — is under structural pressure, and the company is racing to rebuild the model before that spread deflates. Ezzat's long, defensive rebuttal of Palantir's "SAP migration in two weeks" claim ("don't stay on the headline") is the tell that the AI-disruption question is the one that keeps management up at night.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: STRENGTHENING operationally, on a NARROW and structurally exposed moat.** The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: this is a genuinely cheap, well-run, scaled leader that has just re-accelerated — but its moat is switching-cost-and-scale in a business whose core economics (billing labor at a spread) sit directly in the path of AI automation. The cheapness is partly a sector-wide "AI will eat IT services" fear-print shared across the cohort (Accenture, Cognizant have de-rated too), and partly a fair discount for a 9% return on invested capital. Moat type: switching-costs plus scale, but narrow — a 9% return on capital and gen-AI pricing give-backs are not the signature of a widening franchise. Whether AI proves a headwind (bill-rate deflation) or a tailwind (transformation demand, Intelligent Operations) is the terminal-value swing factor and is not yet resolved; treat the secular threat as material, not yet terminal.

bear_thesis: The bear case does not rest on narrative -- it rests on a dated number from the industry's best operator. On 18 June 2026 Accenture fell roughly 19% in a single session, its worst day as a public company, after cutting its fiscal-2026 revenue outlook to +3% to +4% in local currency and disclosing that new bookings fell 2% year on year and managed-services bookings fell 15%. Capgemini dropped more than 8% in Paris the same day, and the entire cohort has since re-rated together. Managed services is the annuity layer of this industry; a 15% decline in its order intake is the first hard evidence that generative artificial intelligence is compressing the value of billable technology labour rather than expanding it. Capgemini's own transcripts corroborate the mechanism from the inside. In February 2025 Charlie Brennan of Jefferies pointed out that with total bookings up 2% and generative-artificial-intelligence bookings contributing 5 points, non-artificial-intelligence bookings must be shrinking; the chief executive did not dispute the arithmetic, answering that 'when we have growth in some areas, it implies that the rest is declining.' The new revenue is substitutional, not additive. On pricing, management has said plainly that productivity gains leak to customers: 'we are customers expect bit by bit cost improvement and efficiency coming from gen AI... we pass some of that to our clients as part of the competitiveness of our offerings.' On market-share wins: taking vendor-consolidation business means 'giving upfront savings. It takes 18 to 24 months to try to recover some of these margins.' A business that cannot keep its own efficiency gains has no pricing power. The balance sheet has weakened sharply into this. Net debt rose from EUR 2.1 billion at the end of 2024 to EUR 5.3 billion on the company's own definition at 31 December 2025, or EUR 6.43 billion including EUR 1.12 billion of lease obligations, after EUR 3.71 billion of acquisitions. Consensus is underwriting a recovery that has not been earned: 2027 net income of EUR 2.25 billion would be 40% above 2025, requiring restructuring to roll off cleanly, WNS synergies to land in full, and bill rates to hold. Finally, the cheapness has already been arbitraged away by the sector selling off together. What would confirm the bear: the 30 July 2026 first-half print showing book-to-bill below 1.0, any cut to the 2026 organic growth or margin guidance, or a first-half net debt figure above EUR 7.5 billion.

interrogator_dossier:
# Capgemini SE (CAP.PA) — a deep dive on management and the setup

**Prepared:** 27 July 2026 · **Transcripts reviewed:** five consecutive calls, February 2025 (full-year 2024) through February 2026 (full-year 2025) · **Price used:** €95.44 on Euronext Paris, intraday 27 July 2026

---

## 1. Narrative arc

Across these five calls the story travels a full arc: from apology, to repair, to reinvention — and the reinvention is being sold into a market that has stopped believing the whole industry.

**February 2025 (full-year 2024) — the apology.** Chief executive Aiman Ezzat opened by conceding the year had gone wrong: "the market proved weaker than we anticipated at the beginning of the year. Clients did not increase their discretionary spend." Revenue fell 2% at constant currency. The emphasis was defensive — resilience, cost discipline, four internal "areas of focus" to simplify the operation. Generative artificial intelligence (software that produces text, code or images on demand) was introduced as a proof point rather than a growth engine, at roughly 4% of full-year bookings.

**April 2025 (first quarter) — the stabilisation.** The language shifted from damage control to trend-spotting: France "has now past the trough," North America "back to slight growth." A genuinely new growth driver was introduced for the first time — European defence, disclosed at "about €1 billion of revenue in European defence, up 12% year-on-year." This is the single most important addition of the whole sequence, because it is the one demand pool that does not depend on corporate information-technology budgets.

**July 2025 (first half) — the pivot is named.** The group returned to growth (+0.7% at constant currency in the second quarter) and Ezzat named the destination: "Intelligent Operations," to be bought rather than built, via the acquisition of WNS, an outsourcing company. The framing changed from selling technology projects to running clients' business processes outright.

**October 2025 (third quarter) — conviction.** Growth accelerated to +2.9% at constant currency, WNS closed, and the pitch hardened into a thesis about where value migrates: clients "are looking for a partner who cannot only run their business processes, but who can fundamentally transform their operation," with a shift "to outcome-based pricing for next-gen intellectual-property-led services."

**February 2026 (full-year 2025) — proof, and a bill.** Revenue grew 3.4% at constant currency, the fourth quarter grew 10.6% including acquisitions, and the group announced its first "mega deal" of over €600 million on "a non-full-time-equivalent based commercial model" — that is, priced on outcomes rather than headcount. Simultaneously it announced "Fit for Growth," a restructuring programme costing "approximately €700 million over the next two years, with the majority in 2026."

**What was quietly dropped:** the 2024-era framing of generative artificial intelligence as an incremental bookings category simply disappears. By the final call it is not a product line but the ground the company stands on — and the restructuring charge is the admission that the existing workforce was built for a different business.

---

## 2. Claims versus financials (forensic)

Management's biggest claims tested against the numbers. The screener's fundamentals block carries two figures I could not reconcile and have corrected from source data — those corrections are flagged, because both would have flattered the case.

| Management claim | Where said | The evidence | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| "Growth rate gradually improved quarter after quarter" | Full-year 2025 call | Constant-currency growth ran −3.3% → −1.1% → −0.4% → +0.7% → +2.9% → +10.6%, then +11.0% in the first quarter of 2026 | **Holds.** Six consecutive quarters of improvement is not a value trap's income statement |
| Operating margin resilient at 13.3% | Full-year 2025 call | Delivered 13.3%, guided to 13.6–13.8% for 2026 | **Holds, but at the low end** — the 2025 target was 13.3–13.5% and they landed on the floor |
| Organic free cash flow "around €1.9 billion" | Repeated all year | €1,949 million delivered | **Holds** |
| Earnings per share growing | Full-year 2025 call, "+5.8%" | Normalised earnings per share €12.95. But basic earnings per share was €9.13, and net profit *fell* from €1.671 billion (2024) to €1.601 billion (2025) | **Diverges.** The headline grows only because it excludes restructuring and acquisition amortisation — costs this company incurs every single year |
| The business earns good returns | Implied throughout | Return on invested capital 8.6% (trailing twelve months), against roughly 8% cost of capital. Goodwill rose from €12.34 billion to €14.86 billion in one year; tangible book value is *negative* €4.3 billion | **Diverges materially.** Growth is being purchased, not compounded |
| Generative artificial intelligence is a margin opportunity | Full-year 2024 call | Ezzat, unprompted: "customers expect bit by bit cost improvement and efficiency coming from gen AI… we pass some of that to our clients" | **The story is poorer than told.** Productivity gains leak to clients |
| "Solid" bookings | Every call | Book-to-bill 1.08 for 2025, 1.21 in the fourth quarter | **Holds** — and this is the number that matters most on 30 July |

**Two screener figures corrected from source.** The scan's "trailing twelve-month free cash flow €4.31 billion" is wrong: audited 2025 operating cash flow was €2.467 billion less €287 million of capital spending, or €2.18 billion, and the company's own organic free cash flow measure was €1.949 billion. The scan's "trailing twelve-month diluted earnings per share €16.55" is likewise unsupportable against a €1.601 billion net profit on roughly 166 million shares. Both errors make the stock look about twice as cheap as it is, and the scan's headline "margin of safety 86%" and "price-to-free-cash-flow 6.7x" inherit the mistake. On real numbers the shares trade at about 8.1 times organic free cash flow and about 11.4 times that figure on an enterprise-value basis (market value plus net debt).

---

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising — and unusually well-calibrated.** This is the strongest single feature of the sequence.

- **February 2025:** flatly defensive. "The market proved weaker than we anticipated."
- **April 2025:** confident but deliberately deflating his own good news, twice. "Let's not consider something has gone much, much better. So it is slightly better." Asked whether guidance was conservative: "You don't expect me to be [indiscernible], so it's between realistic and conservative."
- **July 2025:** the first forward-leaning language — "We see the benefits of the actions announced in the third quarter of 2024."
- **October 2025:** "Q3 was a strong quarter for the group better than expected."
- **February 2026:** assertive and specific — "2026 is really the moment of truth for AI," plus a first-quarter growth range given to the half-point (8.5% to 9.5% at constant currency).

The shift from defensive vocabulary (efficiency, cost, resilience) to offensive vocabulary (mega deal, growth pillars, structural growth opportunity) is real and tracks the numbers rather than running ahead of them. Chief financial officer Nive Bhagat is consistently the more conservative voice — asked in July 2025 whether the cash-flow target held, she gave the least promotional answer in the whole file: "it is definitely challenging but feasible… it takes a lot of fiscal discipline to be able to do it."

---

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High.**

The 2025 sequence is a textbook of cautious guidance beaten in small increments. The year opened with a wide −2% to +2% constant-currency range; the first half came in "slightly better than anticipated"; in July the range was *narrowed* to −1% to +1% while the acquisition contribution was cut from 1–2 points to about 1 point — that is, the underlying target was raised while the headline looked unchanged, and management said so plainly. The year finished "above the upgraded guidance." Margin and cash-flow targets were both hit. In April 2026 the 2026 outlook was *raised* to +6.5% to +8.5% at constant currency.

There is a mild sandbagging pattern, which is a feature rather than a flaw. Two blemishes, both worth pricing:

- **The France call was wrong.** In April 2025 Ezzat was categorical — "France has now past the trough." By July, Harry Read of Rothschild & Co Redburn pushed back that growth was still around −5%, and Ezzat conceded: "I think we have a broad weakness in France." France was still described as "challenging at year-end" in February 2026. That is four quarters of an over-optimistic call.
- **The buyback under-delivered.** In July 2025 the €2 billion repurchase programme was discussed at length. Actual 2025 execution: €542 million, of which €342 million merely neutralised employee-share-plan dilution — roughly €200 million of genuine share-count reduction against a €15.9 billion company. The company was still buying stock in the week of 13–17 July 2026, but the pace is not one that forces anything.

---

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three questions recur, and management's answers get thinner each time.

**Who pays for artificial intelligence, and does it grow the pie or cannibalise it?** Charlie Brennan of Jefferies put the sharpest version in February 2025: bookings grew 2% in the fourth quarter while generative-artificial-intelligence bookings contributed 5 points — "That implies that non-gen AI bookings are actually down." Ezzat did not rebut the arithmetic. He reframed: "when we have growth in some areas, it implies that the rest is declining." That is a concession dressed as an answer, and it is the single most important exchange in the file — it says the new revenue is substitutional, not additive.

**Does artificial-intelligence productivity accrue to Capgemini or to the client?** Asked directly by Ben Castillo-Bernaus of BNP Paribas (February 2025) and again in July 2025. Both times the answer was that savings are shared with clients as a matter of competitiveness. Management has never claimed it captures the gains.

**Vendor consolidation.** Brennan again, July 2025, with the best question of the sequence: "everyone seems to be claiming they are a beneficiary… arithmetically, it feels like someone should be losing." Ezzat's answer was honest and unflattering: winning consolidation means "giving upfront savings. It takes 18 to 24 months to try to recover some of these margins… it tends to have a negative impact on the gross margin side."

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** the headcount-to-revenue link. Michael Briest of UBS asked directly in February 2026 how headcount develops. Ezzat's answer — "over the midterm… we will see an increase of revenue per head count" — is the right ambition but carries no timeline, no target, and no disclosure that would let anyone verify it.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Generative-artificial-intelligence savings are passed to clients** (February 2025, July 2025). A business without pricing power over its own productivity gains.

🔴 **Vendor-consolidation wins depress gross margin for 18–24 months** (July 2025). Market-share gains are bought.

🔴 **€700 million restructuring to "realign capabilities"** (February 2026). The plainest admission in the file that the existing skill base is being obsoleted by the technology the company sells.

🔴 **Return on invested capital of 8.6% against a roughly 8% cost of capital**, with goodwill up €2.5 billion in a year and negative tangible book value. Growth by acquisition at bare-minimum returns.

🔴 **France weak for six straight quarters** after being called past its trough.

🟢 **Six consecutive quarters of accelerating revenue**, ending at +11.0% at constant currency in the first quarter of 2026, with guidance raised in April 2026.

🟢 **European defence: roughly €1 billion of revenue growing double digits** (April 2025, reaffirmed February 2026) with management expecting "further acceleration in the next 2 to 3 years." This demand pool is genuinely uncorrelated to corporate technology budgets.

🟢 **The €600 million mega deal on a non-headcount commercial model** (February 2026). This is the most important green flag in the file: it is direct evidence that the company can sell outcomes rather than hours — the exact transition the bear case says it cannot make.

🟢 **Guidance delivered on all three 2025 targets** and consistently under-promised.

Asked to respond to a competitor's claim of radically compressed migration timelines, Ezzat gave a specific, technical, non-defensive rebuttal — "it's not going to make your SAP migration in 2 weeks" — and explained the applicability limits. ## 7. Hidden signals

**The unit of sale changed.** Across five calls the vocabulary moves from "projects" and "programmes" (2024) to "processes" and "operations" (2025) to "outcomes" (2026). A company that sells hours is describing itself as a company that sells results. That is either the correct adaptation to a world where hours are deflating, or the language a business adopts when it can no longer defend its hourly rate. The €600 million non-headcount contract is the first hard evidence for the optimistic reading.

**"Structural," used about a customer, is a warning.** On automotive (October 2025): "what we see in auto is a structural change in terms of demand, but also in terms of delivery model… engineering tend to be traditionally delivered onshore… and that's really moving away from there." Read carefully, that is a description of the same offshore-deflation force the market fears will be applied to Capgemini itself.

**The chief financial officer's silence on 2026 margin drivers.** Asked in October 2025 for the puts and takes on 2026 margin, Bhagat repeated the 2025 answer nearly verbatim — mix shift, operating effectiveness, selling and administrative costs. No new lever was named for a year in which €700 million of restructuring would be spent.

**Capital allocation shifted from shareholders to acquisitions.** Buybacks ran €876 million (2023) and €989 million (2024), then fell to €542 million in 2025 — the year €3.71 billion went out the door on acquisitions and net debt more than doubled. The stated €2 billion programme has been outbid by the deal pipeline.

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a decaying business. Revenue is accelerating, bookings are healthy, guidance has been raised, and cash generation is steady at roughly €1.9 billion a year. But the company is deliberately rebuilding what it sells and how it charges for it, funding that rebuild with €700 million of restructuring and €3.7 billion of acquisitions, and levering the balance sheet to do it — net debt went from €2.1 billion to €5.3 billion on the company's own measure (€6.43 billion including lease obligations) in a single year.

Every close comparable has since re-rated together, and on live multiples Capgemini is no longer cheap against them: it trades at roughly 7.5 times equity free cash flow versus Accenture at about 7.5 times, Cognizant at about 9 times and Sopra Steria at about 6.4 times, while carrying the lowest returns and the only leveraged balance sheet in the group. The discount the screener detected has already been arbitraged away by the whole cohort de-rating together. What remains is a bet on one shared question — whether artificial intelligence deflates billable technology labour — and that bet pays off or fails for every name in the group at once.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is switching costs — Capgemini is embedded in clients' core enterprise systems, and the Netherlands Police and sovereign-cloud contracts show those relationships are sticky and multi-year. But width must be judged on returns, and the returns say the moat is thin and thinning: return on invested capital of 8.6% is at or below the cost of capital, it has fallen as acquisitions loaded on goodwill, and management has stated on the record that productivity gains are passed to clients. A business that cannot keep its own efficiency savings does not have pricing power.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The threat is the automation of information-technology and outsourcing headcount — the deflation of a business model that bills labour hours at a spread, made worse by the WNS acquisition adding a large outsourcing base at exactly the layer most exposed to automation. The evidence is dated and real, not narrative: Accenture's bookings crack on 18 June 2026 is the sector's first hard number. But three things argue against terminal impairment — revenue is accelerating rather than declining, roughly €1 billion of double-digit-growth European defence work sits outside corporate technology budgets entirely, and the €600 million outcome-priced contract shows the company can monetise the transition rather than only suffer it.

**Fear print or value trap? Neither cleanly — it is a fairly-priced franchise inside a de-rated cohort.** The cheapness is real against history and largely absent against live peers. That is not a mispricing to harvest; it is a sector-wide repricing to have a view on.

Both errors make the stock look about twice as cheap as it is, and the scan's headline "margin of safety 86%" and "price-to-free-cash-flow 6.7x" inherit the mistake. On real numbers the shares trade at about 8.1 times organic free cash flow and about 11.4 times that figure on an enterprise-value basis (market value plus net debt).

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Rising — and unusually well-calibrated.** This is the strongest single feature of the sequence.

- **February 2025:** flatly defensive. "The market proved weaker than we anticipated."
- **April 2025:** confident but deliberately deflating his own good news, twice. "Let's not consider something has gone much, much better. So it is slightly better." Asked whether guidance was conservative: "You don't expect me to be [indiscernible], so it's between realistic and conservative."
- **July 2025:** the first forward-leaning language — "We see the benefits of the actions announced in the third quarter of 2024."
- **October 2025:** "Q3 was a strong quarter for the group better than expected."
- **February 2026:** assertive and specific — "2026 is really the moment of truth for AI," plus a first-quarter growth range given to the half-point (8.5% to 9.5% at constant currency).

The shift from defensive vocabulary (efficiency, cost, resilience) to offensive vocabulary (mega deal, growth pillars, structural growth opportunity) is real and tracks the numbers rather than running ahead of them. Chief financial officer Nive Bhagat is consistently the more conservative voice — asked in July 2025 whether the cash-flow target held, she gave the least promotional answer in the whole file: "it is definitely challenging but feasible… it takes a lot of fiscal discipline to be able to do it."

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: High.**

The 2025 sequence is a textbook of cautious guidance beaten in small increments. The year opened with a wide −2% to +2% constant-currency range; the first half came in "slightly better than anticipated"; in July the range was *narrowed* to −1% to +1% while the acquisition contribution was cut from 1–2 points to about 1 point — that is, the underlying target was raised while the headline looked unchanged, and management said so plainly. The year finished "above the upgraded guidance." Margin and cash-flow targets were both hit. In April 2026 the 2026 outlook was *raised* to +6.5% to +8.5% at constant currency.

There is a mild sandbagging pattern, which is a feature rather than a flaw. Two blemishes, both worth pricing:

- **The France call was wrong.** In April 2025 Ezzat was categorical — "France has now past the trough." By July, Harry Read of Rothschild & Co Redburn pushed back that growth was still around −5%, and Ezzat conceded: "I think we have a broad weakness in France." France was still described as "challenging at year-end" in February 2026. That is four quarters of an over-optimistic call.
- **The buyback under-delivered.** In July 2025 the €2 billion repurchase programme was discussed at length. Actual 2025 execution: €542 million, of which €342 million merely neutralised employee-share-plan dilution — roughly €200 million of genuine share-count reduction against a €15.9 billion company. The company was still buying stock in the week of 13–17 July 2026, but the pace is not one that forces anything.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

Three questions recur, and management's answers get thinner each time.

**Who pays for artificial intelligence, and does it grow the pie or cannibalise it?** Charlie Brennan of Jefferies put the sharpest version in February 2025: bookings grew 2% in the fourth quarter while generative-artificial-intelligence bookings contributed 5 points — "That implies that non-gen AI bookings are actually down." Ezzat did not rebut the arithmetic. He reframed: "when we have growth in some areas, it implies that the rest is declining." That is a concession dressed as an answer, and it is the single most important exchange in the file — it says the new revenue is substitutional, not additive.

**Does artificial-intelligence productivity accrue to Capgemini or to the client?** Asked directly by Ben Castillo-Bernaus of BNP Paribas (February 2025) and again in July 2025. Both times the answer was that savings are shared with clients as a matter of competitiveness. Management has never claimed it captures the gains.

**Vendor consolidation.** Brennan again, July 2025, with the best question of the sequence: "everyone seems to be claiming they are a beneficiary… arithmetically, it feels like someone should be losing." Ezzat's answer was honest and unflattering: winning consolidation means "giving upfront savings. It takes 18 to 24 months to try to recover some of these margins… it tends to have a negative impact on the gross margin side."

**What analysts worry about that management is not addressing:** the headcount-to-revenue link. Michael Briest of UBS asked directly in February 2026 how headcount develops. Ezzat's answer — "over the midterm… we will see an increase of revenue per head count" — is the right ambition but carries no timeline, no target, and no disclosure that would let anyone verify it.

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Non-artificial-intelligence bookings are shrinking** (February 2025, unrebutted). The growth engine is being fed by the rest of the portfolio.

🔴 **Generative-artificial-intelligence savings are passed to clients** (February 2025, July 2025). A business without pricing power over its own productivity gains.

🔴 **Vendor-consolidation wins depress gross margin for 18–24 months** (July 2025). Market-share gains are bought.

🔴 **€700 million restructuring to "realign capabilities"** (February 2026). The plainest admission in the file that the existing skill base is being obsoleted by the technology the company sells.

🔴 **Return on invested capital of 8.6% against a roughly 8% cost of capital**, with goodwill up €2.5 billion in a year and negative tangible book value. Growth by acquisition at bare-minimum returns.

🔴 **France weak for six straight quarters** after being called past its trough.

🟢 **Six consecutive quarters of accelerating revenue**, ending at +11.0% at constant currency in the first quarter of 2026, with guidance raised in April 2026.

🟢 **European defence: roughly €1 billion of revenue growing double digits** (April 2025, reaffirmed February 2026) with management expecting "further acceleration in the next 2 to 3 years." This demand pool is genuinely uncorrelated to corporate technology budgets.

🟢 **The €600 million mega deal on a non-headcount commercial model** (February 2026). This is the most important green flag in the file: it is direct evidence that the company can sell outcomes rather than hours — the exact transition the bear case says it cannot make.

🟢 **Guidance delivered on all three 2025 targets** and consistently under-promised.

🟢 **The Palantir answer** (February 2026). Asked to respond to a competitor's claim of radically compressed migration timelines, Ezzat gave a specific, technical, non-defensive rebuttal — "it's not going to make your SAP migration in 2 weeks" — and explained the applicability limits. That is what a confident operator sounds like; it is not proof he is right.

## 7. Hidden signals

**The unit of sale changed.** Across five calls the vocabulary moves from "projects" and "programmes" (2024) to "processes" and "operations" (2025) to "outcomes" (2026). A company that sells hours is describing itself as a company that sells results. That is either the correct adaptation to a world where hours are deflating, or the language a business adopts when it can no longer defend its hourly rate. The €600 million non-headcount contract is the first hard evidence for the optimistic reading.

**"Structural," used about a customer, is a warning.** On automotive (October 2025): "what we see in auto is a structural change in terms of demand, but also in terms of delivery model… engineering tend to be traditionally delivered onshore… and that's really moving away from there." Read carefully, that is a description of the same offshore-deflation force the market fears will be applied to Capgemini itself.

**The chief financial officer's silence on 2026 margin drivers.** Asked in October 2025 for the puts and takes on 2026 margin, Bhagat repeated the 2025 answer nearly verbatim — mix shift, operating effectiveness, selling and administrative costs. No new lever was named for a year in which €700 million of restructuring would be spent.

**Capital allocation shifted from shareholders to acquisitions.** Buybacks ran €876 million (2023) and €989 million (2024), then fell to €542 million in 2025 — the year €3.71 billion went out the door on acquisitions and net debt more than doubled. The stated €2 billion programme has been outbid by the deal pipeline.

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a decaying business. Revenue is accelerating, bookings are healthy, guidance has been raised, and cash generation is steady at roughly €1.9 billion a year. But the company is deliberately rebuilding what it sells and how it charges for it, funding that rebuild with €700 million of restructuring and €3.7 billion of acquisitions, and levering the balance sheet to do it — net debt went from €2.1 billion to €5.3 billion on the company's own measure (€6.43 billion including lease obligations) in a single year.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing:** the apparent cheapness is not company-specific. On 18 June 2026 Accenture — the sector's benchmark — fell about 19% in a day after cutting its outlook and disclosing that managed-services bookings had dropped 15% year on year; Capgemini fell more than 8% the same session. Every close comparable has since re-rated together, and on live multiples Capgemini is no longer cheap against them: it trades at roughly 7.5 times equity free cash flow versus Accenture at about 7.5 times, Cognizant at about 9 times and Sopra Steria at about 6.4 times, while carrying the lowest returns and the only leveraged balance sheet in the group. The discount the screener detected has already been arbitraged away by the whole cohort de-rating together. What remains is a bet on one shared question — whether artificial intelligence deflates billable technology labour — and that bet pays off or fails for every name in the group at once.

**Economic moat: ERODING.** The moat type is switching costs — Capgemini is embedded in clients' core enterprise systems, and the Netherlands Police and sovereign-cloud contracts show those relationships are sticky and multi-year. But width must be judged on returns, and the returns say the moat is thin and thinning: return on invested capital of 8.6% is at or below the cost of capital, it has fallen as acquisitions loaded on goodwill, and management has stated on the record that productivity gains are passed to clients. A business that cannot keep its own efficiency savings does not have pricing power.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The threat is the automation of information-technology and outsourcing headcount — the deflation of a business model that bills labour hours at a spread, made worse by the WNS acquisition adding a large outsourcing base at exactly the layer most exposed to automation. The evidence is dated and real, not narrative: Accenture's bookings crack on 18 June 2026 is the sector's first hard number. But three things argue against terminal impairment — revenue is accelerating rather than declining, roughly €1 billion of double-digit-growth European defence work sits outside corporate technology budgets entirely, and the €600 million outcome-priced contract shows the company can monetise the transition rather than only suffer it.

**Fear print or value trap? Neither cleanly — it is a fairly-priced franchise inside a de-rated cohort.** The cheapness is real against history and largely absent against live peers. That is not a mispricing to harvest; it is a sector-wide repricing to have a view on.
